author: A Robot
objectives: Represent 2D vectors by magnitude/direction and by horizontal/vertical components.
Add vectors graphically using the tip-to-tail method to find a resultant.
Decompose vectors into components using right-triangle trigonometry and reconstruct vectors from components.
Explain the independence of horizontal and vertical motion in projectile motion.
Describe how velocity components and position change throughout a projectile's flight.
Predict how launch angle and speed affect trajectory, range, and maximum height.

modules.moduleName: Vector Basics: Magnitude, Direction, and Addition
modules.description: Introduces vectors as arrows with magnitude and direction, and demonstrates tip-to-tail vector addition to find a resultant.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Represent a 2D vector by its magnitude and direction.
Add two vectors graphically using the tip-to-tail method.
Identify the resultant vector of a vector sum.
instructions: Observe the two vectors labeled A and B.
Watch as vector B is moved tip-to-tail with vector A to form the resultant vector R.

clips.changeMeaning: Initial staging: two vectors A and B appear at separate positions with labels, and a caption introduces the concept of vectors.
clips.narration: In physics, a vector is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction, like velocity or force. Here we see two vectors, A and B, represented as arrows. The length of each arrow shows its magnitude, and the way it points shows its direction.

components.text: Sliding B to the tip of A

clips.changeMeaning: Vector B moves from its original position so its tail touches the tip of vector A, demonstrating the tip-to-tail placement for addition.
clips.narration: To add vector B to vector A, we slide B so that its tail starts at the tip of A, without changing its length or direction. This is the tip-to-tail method of vector addition.

clips.changeMeaning: The resultant vector R appears, scaled and rotated to visually span from the tail of A to the tip of B, illustrating the sum of the two vectors.
clips.narration: The resultant vector R is drawn from the tail of A to the tip of B. This single vector represents the combined effect of adding A and B together.

modules.description: Shows how a single vector can be decomposed into horizontal and vertical components using right-triangle trigonometry, and how those components reconstruct the original vector.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Decompose a vector into x- and y-components using right-triangle trigonometry.
Reconstruct a vector's magnitude and direction from its components.
Relate the angle of a vector to the ratio of its components.
instructions: Watch vector V being decomposed into its horizontal (Vx) and vertical (Vy) components.
Observe how the right triangle formed by Vx, Vy, and V relates to trigonometric functions.

clips.changeMeaning: Vector V is displayed at an angle to set up the decomposition demonstration; caption introduces the concept of components.
clips.narration: Any vector can be broken down into two perpendicular pieces called components. Here is vector V, pointing up and to the right at some angle theta above the horizontal.

clips.changeMeaning: The horizontal component vector Vx grows into view along the x-axis beneath V, showing the projection of V's magnitude along the horizontal.
clips.narration: The horizontal component, Vx, is the projection of V onto the x-axis. Its length equals the magnitude of V times the cosine of theta.

clips.changeMeaning: The vertical component vector Vy grows into view along the y-axis at the tip of Vx, completing the right triangle with V as the hypotenuse.
clips.narration: The vertical component, Vy, is the projection of V onto the y-axis. Its length equals the magnitude of V times the sine of theta. Together, Vx and Vy form the two legs of a right triangle with V as the hypotenuse.

clips.changeMeaning: Caption updates to summarize the Pythagorean and inverse-tangent relationships that reconstruct V's magnitude and angle from its components; no geometry changes, reinforcing the math already shown.
clips.narration: Using the Pythagorean theorem, the magnitude of V equals the square root of Vx squared plus Vy squared. And the angle theta equals the inverse tangent of Vy over Vx. This lets us move freely between a vector's magnitude-direction form and its component form.

modules.moduleName: Projectile Motion: Independent Horizontal and Vertical Components
modules.description: Demonstrates how a projectile's initial velocity vector decomposes into constant horizontal and changing vertical components, producing a parabolic trajectory.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent.
Describe how horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical velocity changes under gravity.
Identify the point of maximum height as where vertical velocity equals zero.
instructions: Watch the projectile launch and observe its velocity vector components throughout the flight.
Notice how the horizontal arrow stays the same length while the vertical arrow shrinks, vanishes, then grows in the opposite direction.

clips.changeMeaning: The cannon, ball, and both velocity component arrows are staged at the launch point, introducing the decomposition of initial velocity before motion begins.
clips.narration: Let's launch a projectile at an angle. Its initial velocity vector can be split into a horizontal component, vx, and a vertical component, vy, just like any other vector.

clips.changeMeaning: The ball moves upward and to the right along the first half of its arc; the horizontal velocity arrow keeps constant length while the vertical velocity arrow visibly shortens, showing deceleration due to gravity.
clips.narration: As the projectile rises, notice that the horizontal component vx stays exactly the same length throughout the flight, because no horizontal force acts on the projectile. Meanwhile, the vertical component vy shrinks as gravity decelerates the upward motion.

clips.changeMeaning: The ball reaches the top of its arc; the vertical velocity arrow shrinks to near-zero length, illustrating the instant of maximum height, while the horizontal arrow remains unchanged.
clips.narration: At the peak of the trajectory, the vertical velocity momentarily reaches zero. This is the moment of maximum height. The horizontal velocity, however, is still nonzero and unchanged.

components.text: Falling: vx constant, vy grows downward

clips.changeMeaning: The ball descends toward the ground along the second half of the arc; the vertical velocity arrow reappears pointing downward and grows in length, while the horizontal arrow stays constant, completing the parabolic path.
clips.narration: As the projectile falls, the vertical component grows again but now points downward, while the horizontal component remains constant. The result is the familiar curved, parabolic path of a projectile.

modules.description: Lets students manipulate launch angle and speed to observe effects on trajectory, range, and maximum height, and identify the angle of maximum range.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict how launch angle affects trajectory shape, range, and maximum height.
Predict how launch speed affects range and maximum height.
Identify the launch angle that produces maximum range for a given speed.
instructions: Adjust the launch angle dial to see how the trajectory changes.
Compare trajectories at low, 45-degree, and high launch angles.
Observe which angle produces the greatest range.

components.text: Compare trajectories at different launch angles
Low angle (20 deg): short, flat trajectory

clips.changeMeaning: A low-angle trajectory line is drawn and displayed, showing a flat arc with limited height and range, establishing the baseline comparison case.
clips.narration: Now let's explore how launch angle affects a projectile's path. Here is a low-angle launch, around 20 degrees above the horizontal. Notice the flat, low trajectory with a short time of flight.

components.text: 45 degrees: maximum range for this speed

clips.changeMeaning: A second trajectory line for a 45-degree launch appears alongside the low-angle one, visually demonstrating that this angle yields the greatest horizontal range for the same speed.
clips.narration: Now compare that to a 45-degree launch. For a given launch speed, this angle produces the maximum possible range, balancing height and horizontal distance perfectly.

components.text: Steep angle (70 deg): high, but shorter range

clips.changeMeaning: A third trajectory line for a steep 70-degree launch appears, showing a tall but short-range arc, completing the three-way comparison of low, optimal, and steep launch angles.
clips.narration: Finally, here is a steep 70-degree launch. The projectile reaches a much greater height, but its range is shorter than the 45-degree case, because so much of the initial speed is directed vertically rather than horizontally.

components.text: Try it yourself: drag the cannon to change angle

clips.changeMeaning: The cannon becomes draggable for free exploration, inviting students to test different angles themselves while the caption summarizes the effect of speed on range and height.
clips.narration: Try dragging the cannon to change its angle yourself, and imagine how increasing the launch speed would stretch all three trajectories further, while keeping their relative shapes the same. A faster launch increases both range and maximum height, but the 45-degree angle remains optimal for range at any given speed.
